pathway.question: Should we own this issuer, in which instrument, and why?

runs.text: - Year-end credit metrics are strong and improving. Net debt was 1.14x EBITDA against 1.88x a year earlier, EBITDA covered cash interest 11.79x against 9.57x, and total debt fell from USD 2,988.3 million to USD 2,501.7 million as working capital released cash. Creditors are well covered on the 2026 year-end balance sheet. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation B01; calculation B02; calculation B03

- The year end is the seasonal low for debt, so leverage through the year is higher. Net debt was USD 3,879.3 million at the February 28, 2026 quarter end, 1.73 times the year-end level, and the securitization and repurchase facilities were used to USD 850.0 million and USD 250.0 million at quarter ends; both run only to August 25, 2027, so receivables funding is a recurring renewal exposure. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-02-28_chscp-20260228.htm.jsonl, pages 12–13; 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 164; calculation B04; calculation B14

- Earnings quality is lower than the ratios suggest because 28.9% of EBITDA is equity income and CF Nitrogen alone supplied 36.0% of pre-tax earnings. Distributions exceeded equity income by USD 25.4 million in FY2026, so the income was cash-backed, but it follows urea and UAN prices and the interest is a 7.86% stake CHS cannot control. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 158; calculation B06

- The swing factor is Energy, where policy decides part of the margin. Energy earned USD 554.6 million before tax against a USD 19.0 million loss in FY2025, helped by about USD 205.0 million of small refinery exemption relief; a repeat of the FY2025 margin would remove most of the FY2026 earnings uplift. Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 64; 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 67; calculation B07

- Liquidity is adequate on committed lines and the maturity profile is gentle. Cash of USD 263.6 million sits beside an undrawn USD 2,800.0 million revolver that expires April 21, 2028; the notes are USD 1,703.0 million of unsecured private placements and a USD 300.0 million term loan, with USD 450.0 million due in fiscal 2030 the largest scheduled year. Letters of credit under the revolver are not stated, so availability net of them is not established. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, pages 163–165; calculation B05; calculation B13

- Financial policy is the discretionary lever and it is turning. The fiscal 2027 plan absorbs USD 1,361.3 million of capital spending, major maintenance, preferred dividends and member payouts, which FY2026 operating cash flow of USD 1,584.0 million covers by USD 222.7 million but FY2025 operating cash flow of USD 635.8 million would miss by USD 725.5 million; the board can cut payouts but has just signalled a rise. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 76; EX-99.1_2026-11-04_a4qfy26earningrelease.htm.jsonl, page 1; calculation B08

- Counting the USD 2,264.0 million of preferred stock as debt-like lifts FY2026 net leverage to 2.29x, so creditors rank ahead of a large fixed claim that is junior to them but carries USD 168.7 million of dividends a year. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, pages 170–171; calculation B10

runs.text: CHS's main strengths are financial, not competitive. Low year-end leverage and high interest cover let it absorb one weak year without refinancing pressure, as net debt of 1.14x EBITDA and cover of 11.79x show. A USD 2,800.0 million undrawn committed revolver and a long-dated unsecured note stack mean no large maturity wall, with USD 450.0 million the largest year. Member equity of 57.90% of assets and board-discretionary redemption of equity certificates give a buffer. Scale, with USD 39.2 billion of revenue across energy, grains and crop inputs, spreads exposure across three commodity chains. Finally, there is no sponsor, so value extraction by an owner is not a documented risk. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 144; 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, pages 163–165; calculation B01; calculation B05; calculation B13

Its main weaknesses are earnings volatility and seasonal reliance on short-term funding. Gross margin is thin at 4.56% of revenue and operating margin only 1.51%, so a small price or volume move changes earnings sharply. Half of pre-tax earnings is equity income from joint ventures CHS does not control, led by CF Nitrogen. Energy earnings depend on refining margins, renewable energy credit costs and refinery exemptions that may not recur. Seasonal borrowing lifts net debt to 1.73 times its year-end level, funded partly by receivables facilities that need renewal by August 2027. Capital spending and member payouts are both set to rise while farm demand is weak, and covenant levels are unknown. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 60; 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 64; calculation B04; calculation B11

runs.text: CHS announced no merger, sponsor transaction or acquisition in the filings for FY2026. It finished its exit from the Producer Ag joint venture on December 31, 2025, taking working capital, mainly inventory and cash, for its equity interest and amounts previously owed, with no effect on the FY2026 income statement. In FY2025 it paid USD 237.2 million for business acquisitions, and the annual report ties goodwill of USD 59.5 million that year to the acquisition of West Central Ag Services. Basis: 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 159; 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 146; 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 161; 10-Q_2025-11-30_chscp-20251130.htm.jsonl, page 8

No new note issue appears for FY2026. The USD 80.0 million of notes due in fiscal 2026 were repaid, leaving private placement notes at USD 1,703.0 million. The new term debt was a USD 300.0 million draw on the revolving term facility between November 30, 2025 and February 28, 2026, which reverts to a nonrevolving term loan payable October 29, 2029, and amendments on August 26, 2026 extended the securitization and repurchase facilities to August 25, 2027. Basis: 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, pages 164–165; 10-Q_2025-11-30_chscp-20251130.htm.jsonl, page 13; 10-Q_2026-02-28_chscp-20260228.htm.jsonl, page 13

Two growth projects are announced but not yet approved: a USD 700 million soybean plant in Wisconsin and a USD 450 million phosphate joint venture with OCP North America in Louisiana, both expected in late 2028 or 2029. The company intends USD 300.0 million of fiscal 2027 patronage cash and equity redemptions; none of these is a completed transaction, and no funding plan is stated. Basis: EX-99.1_2026-11-04_a4qfy26earningrelease.htm.jsonl, pages 1–2; 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 76

fields.value: CHS carries low leverage at its August 31, 2026 year end, with net debt of USD 2,238.1 million at 1.14x EBITDA, but that is the seasonal low and 28.9% of the EBITDA is equity income, so creditors should underwrite to seasonal-high debt.

fields.value: CHS reports no EBITDA, so the figure used is net income plus interest, tax and depreciation and amortisation. Net debt was USD 3,879.3 million at the February 28, 2026 quarter end, the highest period-end balance in the sources and 1.73 times the year-end level, and Q4 alone produced 65.5% of annual pre-tax earnings.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: - Year-end leverage is low and falling, but it is a seasonal low. Total debt was USD 2,501.7 million at the 2026 year end, 1.27x EBITDA, against 2.12x a year earlier, while the working-capital lines swelled debt to a February quarter-end high. A lender sizing to that high sees 1.73 times the year-end net debt, so the year-end ratio overstates the cushion.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: - The EBITDA behind that leverage is a house calculation and 28.9% of it is equity income from joint ventures. Distributions from investees exceeded equity income by USD 25.4 million in FY2026, and CF Nitrogen alone paid USD 447.3 million, so the income was cash-backed this year, but it depends on urea and UAN prices. On EBITDA excluding equity income and other income, FY2026 total debt is 1.97x.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: - Earnings are back-ended. Q4 pre-tax earnings were USD 739.3 million, 65.5% of the year, after a nine-month operating loss. The annual report's own seasonality table shows Q4 at a much lower share and Q2 as a positive share although Q2 was a loss, so seasonality should be read from the quarterly filings, not from that table.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: - Cash generation was strong but concentrated in Q4. Operating cash flow was USD 1,584.0 million, of which USD 1,382.8 million came in Q4 as receivables unwound and earnings peaked; free cash flow after capital spending and major maintenance was USD 1,052.5 million, and USD 753.4 million after preferred dividends, patronage cash and equity redemptions.

fields.value: Basis: 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 146; 10-Q_2026-05-31_chscp-20260531.htm.jsonl, pages 5–6; calculation C23; calculation C24

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: - Coverage is ample. EBITDA covered cash interest paid 11.79x in FY2026 against 9.57x in FY2025, even though interest expense rose USD 17.6 million on a higher average short-term balance and less capitalised interest.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: - Liquidity rests on a committed revolver and the securitization lines. At year end the USD 2,800.0 million revolver was undrawn alongside USD 263.6 million of cash. The securitization and repurchase facilities, which reached USD 850.0 million and USD 250.0 million of use at quarter ends, run only to August 25, 2027, and letters of credit under the revolver are not stated, so availability net of them is not established.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: - The debt stack is long-dated and unsecured where it is term debt: USD 1,703.0 million of private placement notes and a USD 300.0 million term loan, with USD 450.0 million due in fiscal 2030 as the largest single year. The maturity chart also counts the short-term notes payable in fiscal 2027, so that bar is a rollover need, not scheduled amortisation.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: - Claims on cash are rising. Capital expenditures are expected at USD 850.8 million in FY2027 against USD 463.3 million in FY2026, and the company intends USD 300.0 million of patronage cash and equity redemptions beside USD 168.7 million of preferred dividends. Counting the USD 2,264.0 million of preferred stock as debt-like lifts FY2026 net leverage to 2.29x.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The strongest case against the low-leverage reading is that FY2026 earnings look unusually good for a commodity cooperative. Energy earned USD 554.6 million of pre-tax earnings after a USD 19.0 million loss in FY2025, helped by about USD 205.0 million of small refinery exemption relief, and record renewable energy credit costs were largely offset by higher crack spreads and wider crude oil discounts. If EBITDA returned to the FY2025 level of USD 1,412.3 million, FY2026 year-end total debt would be 1.77x and the February 2026 quarter-end total debt of USD 4,127.8 million would be 2.92x. The view would turn if period-end debt stays near its February level after the fiscal 2027 capital programme starts, if equity distributions from CF Nitrogen fall, or if the covenant levels, which the filings do not give, prove tight against those ratios.

fields.value: Directors are farmer-elected by region, no employee may sit on the board, and preferred holders and lenders have no vote. fields.name: Quote
fields.value: - No sponsor controls CHS, so the usual extraction risk is absent, but control sits with member-elected directors and creditors have no vote. Voting rights arise from membership rather than from equity or debt, the bylaws bar employees from the board, and the board has seventeen seats with one vacant, so the discipline on payouts rests on the board's policy and on debt terms the filings do not show.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: - Member distributions are the financial-policy lever and the board sets them at its discretion. Cash patronage and equity redemptions paid fell from USD 721.9 million in FY2024 to USD 130.4 million in FY2026, which left cash for debt reduction, but the company intends USD 300.0 million in fiscal 2027, USD 150.0 million of patronage cash and up to USD 150.0 million of redemptions, beside USD 168.7 million of preferred dividends a year.

fields.value: - Half of pre-tax earnings is equity income and one joint venture dominates it. The agreement is expected to pay out about USD 35 million a year more than CHS's share of earnings, which runs the carrying value down to zero over the supply agreement's life.

fields.value: - Energy is the swing factor and its earnings depend on policy as well as markets. fields.value: - Grains carries most of the revenue but little of the earnings, at 55.02% of FY2026 revenue and 11.29% of pre-tax earnings, and China's May 2025 suspension of soybean imports from CHS shows its exposure to trade policy. Energy was 28.96% of revenue and 49.13% of earnings, so the revenue mix says little about where creditor cash flow comes from.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The case for lower governance risk is strong. Members own the business and are also its customers and suppliers, total equities of USD 11,644.8 million are 57.90% of assets, and USD 6,256.0 million of patron equity certificates can be redeemed only when the board decides, which cushions creditors in a downturn and was used in FY2026 when payouts were cut. The view would move to higher risk if fiscal 2027 redemptions exceed the USD 150.0 million intended, if CF Nitrogen distributions fall below USD 447.3 million while capital spending rises, or if losses emerge in the CHS Capital book; it would move to lower risk if the debt agreements show distribution limits that bind the board.

fields.value: Fundamental credit view of CHS INC (issuer id chscp), as of 2026-11-05, on the credit_snapshot pathway. Scope: a creditor's synthesis of business risk, earnings durability, liquidity, leverage, refinancing and financial policy from the seven supplied filings and releases and the three earlier analyses, with no rating, security recommendation or sizing.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: CHS has a strong year-end credit profile, with net debt at 1.14x EBITDA and USD 3,063.6 million of cash and undrawn revolver, but its earnings are cyclical and policy-dependent, and seasonal debt, rising capital spending and higher member payouts can erode that cushion.

Covenant levels, ratings and debt agreements are not in the filings, so headroom is not established.

The view would improve if covenant levels show wide headroom, if period-end debt stays well below the February level, or if Energy earnings prove less dependent on exemptions. It would worsen if the securitization and repurchase facilities are not extended beyond August 25, 2027, if equity distributions from CF Nitrogen fall while capital spending runs at USD 850.8 million, or if payouts exceed the USD 300.0 million intended.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: CHS's main strengths are financial, not competitive. Low year-end leverage and high interest cover let it absorb one weak year without refinancing pressure, as net debt of 1.14x EBITDA and cover of 11.79x show. A USD 2,800.0 million undrawn committed revolver and a long-dated unsecured note stack mean no large maturity wall, with USD 450.0 million the largest year. Member equity of 57.90% of assets and board-discretionary redemption of equity certificates give a buffer. Scale, with USD 39.2 billion of revenue across energy, grains and crop inputs, spreads exposure across three commodity chains. Finally, there is no sponsor, so value extraction by an owner is not a documented risk.

fields.value: Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 144; 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, pages 163–165; calculation B01; calculation B05; calculation B13

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Its main weaknesses are earnings volatility and seasonal reliance on short-term funding. Gross margin is thin at 4.56% of revenue and operating margin only 1.51%, so a small price or volume move changes earnings sharply. Half of pre-tax earnings is equity income from joint ventures CHS does not control, led by CF Nitrogen. Energy earnings depend on refining margins, renewable energy credit costs and refinery exemptions that may not recur. Seasonal borrowing lifts net debt to 1.73 times its year-end level, funded partly by receivables facilities that need renewal by August 2027. Capital spending and member payouts are both set to rise while farm demand is weak, and covenant levels are unknown.

fields.value: Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 60; 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 64; calculation B04; calculation B11

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: CHS is a farmer-owned cooperative whose three reportable segments run on commodity spreads. Energy refines about 190,000 barrels a day at Laurel and McPherson, Grains is the largest cooperative marketer and processor of grain and oilseeds, and Agronomy sells crop inputs and holds a 7.86% interest in CF Nitrogen. Revenue is price-driven and thin-margin, so the cash that services debt comes from refining spreads, processing margins and joint venture distributions, not from revenue scale. Grains is 55.02% of revenue but 11.29% of pre-tax earnings, while Energy is 28.96% of revenue and 49.13% of earnings.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: No sponsor, parent or restricted group sits above the issuer. Control rests with member-elected farmer directors, preferred holders and lenders have no vote, and the debt is issued by the consolidated cooperative; CHS Capital, Cofina Funding and the equity-method joint ventures sit below it. For creditors this removes sponsor extraction risk but leaves the board's discretionary payout policy as the financial-policy lever, and the structural position of unsecured notes against receivables-backed financing is not established because no debt agreement is supplied.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Revenue is volatile through price and stable through volume. Revenue fell 9.68% in FY2025 and rose 10.63% in FY2026 on commodity prices while volumes moved less, and the company states it is exposed to weather, trade policy and the farm economy. Because gross margin is only 3.21% to 4.56% of revenue, creditors should read revenue as a driver of working capital, not of earnings.

fields.value: Costs are largely variable commodity inputs, with fixed refinery and processing costs behind them, so margin depends on spreads. Operating margin was 0.26% in FY2025 and 1.51% in FY2026; marketing, general and administrative expense rose 14.3% in FY2026 on incentive pay and software amortisation. This is operating leverage to spreads: refining margin, crush margin and urea prices explain most year-to-year change, which makes margin resilience weak without an offset from equity income.

fields.value: Cash conversion swings with working capital and capital spending. Free cash flow after capital spending and major maintenance was USD 1,052.5 million in FY2026, minus USD 364.2 million in FY2025 and USD 441.4 million in FY2024, and Q4 of FY2026 delivered USD 1,382.8 million of operating cash flow as receivables unwound. Capital spending flexes, since major maintenance fell from USD 271.4 million to USD 68.3 million, but FY2027 plans USD 850.8 million, so conversion in a weak year is the credit test.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Rivalry and buyer power cap pricing. CHS competes with larger, better known companies, its members are not obliged to trade with it, and consolidation among cooperative customers and input manufacturers could remove it from supply chains. Substitution matters mainly to Energy, where lower fuel demand would hit diesel sold to farms. These forces explain why margins are thin and why creditors should not extrapolate FY2026 spreads, but they also spread risk across many customers, none above 10% of receivables.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Policy is a material credit driver here. The EPA's March 2026 renewable volume obligation is the highest ever, renewable credit prices rose 86% and 82%, and the small refinery exemptions that gave about USD 205.0 million of relief in FY2026 depend on petitions CHS may not win again; tax rules for cooperatives and clean fuel credits add further policy sensitivity, and China's 2025 suspension of soybean imports shows trade exposure. These factors can move Energy and Grains earnings by more than the cost of CHS's interest, so they belong in the primary downside path.

fields.value: Strengths: low year-end leverage, large unsecured term debt with no large maturity wall, USD 2,800.0 million of undrawn committed revolver, member equity buffer and board-controlled payouts. Weaknesses: thin margins, half of pre-tax earnings from joint ventures, policy-dependent Energy earnings, seasonal debt and unknown covenants. Opportunities: the Wisconsin soybean plant and phosphate venture could add earnings from late 2028 or 2029 if approved and funded sensibly, and lower major maintenance in fiscal 2027 helps cash. Threats: a repeat of FY2025 margins, loss of CF Nitrogen distributions, non-renewal of the receivables facilities by August 2027, farm credit losses at CHS Capital, and tax or exemption changes.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Scale and market position are strong: revenue of USD 39.2 billion and a leading cooperative position in energy and grains. Competitive advantage is average, resting on member relationships and owned logistics rather than pricing power. Business diversification is average because three chains are diversified but equity income concentrates earnings in one joint venture. Cost and capex flexibility is average, since payouts and growth capital are discretionary while refineries need turnarounds. Margin stability is weak, with gross margin at 3.21% in FY2025 and 4.56% in FY2026. Free cash flow stability is average, from minus USD 364.2 million to USD 1,052.5 million. Ability to refinance is average: long-dated unsecured notes show private market access, but no rating or market data is supplied and the receivables lines renew in 2027. Liquidity is strong at the year end with USD 3,063.6 million of cash and undrawn revolver, subject to unstated letters of credit. Financial policy and governance is average: no sponsor and board control support creditors, but payouts are discretionary and covenants are unseen.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The main support is year-end leverage of 1.27x total debt to EBITDA and cover of 11.79x; the main constraints are earnings concentration and seasonal debt; the trend is better in FY2026 than FY2025 but cyclical; and the key missing datapoints are covenant levels, ratings and debt agreements.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Over twelve to twenty-four months, tailwinds are the company's FY2026 operating cash flow, lower major maintenance of USD 41.8 million, higher crush margins from biofuel policy and CF Nitrogen pricing, while headwinds are weak farm demand, record renewable credit costs, a possible end to exemptions and capital spending of USD 850.8 million. Over three to five years the Wisconsin soybean plant and phosphate venture add capacity from late 2028 or 2029 but raise capital needs first; none of the filings gives a forecast, so the medium-term outlook is qualitative.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The downside is a repeat of FY2025 conditions at peak-season borrowing under the fiscal 2027 plan. The initiating condition is Energy margins falling back as crack spreads and exemptions normalise while farmers defer purchases and trade restrictions persist. The first operating break is Energy and Agronomy earnings; operating cash flow falls to the FY2025 level of USD 635.8 million against USD 1,361.3 million of planned capital spending, major maintenance, preferred dividends and member payouts, a shortfall of USD 725.5 million that is funded by borrowing. Net debt would then be about USD 2,963.6 million at year end, 2.10x FY2025-level EBITDA of USD 1,412.3 million, and about USD 4,604.8 million at the seasonal peak, 3.26x. The revolver of USD 2,800.0 million exceeds the extra borrowing, so liquidity would hold, and the observable triggers are covenant tests, the August 2027 receivables renewal and the April 2028 revolver expiry. Management levers are lower payouts and capital spending, which the board has used before.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Overall, CHS presents a strong business profile on scale and a cooperative structure with no sponsor, but credit quality is constrained by thin and policy-dependent margins, half of pre-tax earnings from joint ventures and seasonal debt that is far above the year-end level. Cash-flow durability appears adequate: cover is high in a good year but free cash flow was negative in FY2025. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on renewing the receivables facilities by August 2027 and the revolver by April 2028 and on covenant headroom that the filings do not show. The primary downside path is a margin downturn that meets peak-season borrowing while payouts and capital spending rise. Further analysis would require the credit agreement, covenant levels, ratings and CHS Capital loan data. Fundamental credit completed. Top risk: policy-dependent Energy margins meeting peak-season borrowing.
